alt: Four cards. Absolute poverty is lacking basic necessities for survival. Relative poverty is falling well below the usual standard of living in a society. Subjective poverty is whether people see themselves as poor. Environmental poverty is living in a poor local environment.
caption: How poverty is defined decides how much of it is found.

alt: Three measures for 1968–69: the state standard found just over 6% in poverty, the relative income standard a little over 9%, and Townsend’s relative deprivation measure more than 22%. Below, his questionnaire method and deprivation index, and the criticism that missing items may reflect choice.
caption: The same society showed 6%, 9% or 22% in poverty depending on the measure.

alt: A cycle: adults living in poverty develop distinct values such as fatalism and living for the present; these are passed to children through socialisation; the next generation stays in poverty, and the cycle repeats.
caption: On this view, values passed between generations keep families poor.

alt: Four steps: higher benefits encourage dependence; self-sufficiency is discouraged and single parents and young people lose interest in jobs; an underclass with an alternative value system grows; it is seen as a burden on taxpayers and a cause of crime. Below, criticisms of Murray’s evidence and his neglect of economic causes.
caption: Murray blames welfare for creating an underclass; critics blame missing economic causes.

alt: Two panels. The culture of poverty blames values such as fatalism and, for Murray and the New Right, welfare dependency. Material deprivation blames low pay, unemployment, low benefits, high housing costs and the costs of disability or caring, and sees any culture as a response to lack of opportunity.
caption: Is poverty caused by the values of the poor, or by a lack of money and jobs?

after: ## How governments have tried to alleviate poverty and unemployment
alt: A timeline: the 1942 Beveridge Report named five giants, the welfare state and NHS followed in 1948, the national minimum wage came in 1999 and Universal Credit from 2013. Below, universal benefits avoid stigma while means-tested selective benefits cost less but can create a poverty trap, followed by three evaluations.
caption: Policies have reduced poverty, but each side of the debate criticises them differently.

alt: One town where generations have not worked is read two ways: Murray blames benefits and values; a structural reading blames the closure of the main employer when production moved abroad. Below, negative and positive impacts of globalisation.
caption: Globalisation supports a structural explanation: the jobs left, not the work ethic.
